sections.history: Kovilvenni, whose older name is Tiruvenniyur, is an ancient Shaiva village near Needamangalam, revered in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar and Appar and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. Over time the village came to be known by its temple as Venniyur and then Koil Venni. The stone temple is of the Chola period with later additions; by tradition the site is held to be of great antiquity, its sthala-purana claiming it has stood through all the ages.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Karumbeswarar. Unusually, the lingam is worshipped in the form of a bound sheaf of sugarcane stems, a distinctive image that gives the lord his name. The goddess Soundaranayagi has her own shrine, and the Nandiyavartham plant is honoured as the sthala vriksham, both recalling the legend of the temple's founding.
sections.legends: The sthala-purana tells of two sage-devotees of Shiva who came upon a self-manifested lingam amid a field thick with sugarcane and nandiyavartham. They fell into dispute over how the lingam should be installed and what name to give the lord; Shiva appeared and settled it, declaring that sugarcane would cover him and be his name, and that the nandiyavartham would be his sacred tree. From karumbu, sugarcane, comes the name Karumbeswarar. From the sweetness of the lord's covering flows the belief that an offering of sugar here relieves diabetes.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam. The sugarcane association gives the temple a steady flow of devotees seeking relief from diabetes, who make their offering of sugar to the lord, and this living custom shapes the temple's daily life more than any single great festival.
sections.experience: Kovilvenni offers the pilgrim an unusual and tender image at the heart of its worship — a lingam in the form of sugarcane, a god who chose sweetness as his covering. The darshan of Karumbeswarar, and the simple offering of sugar for health, give this quiet delta temple a gentle, hopeful character all its own.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Kovilvenni is in Tiruvarur district near Needamangalam, roughly 10 km away and about 25 km from Thanjavur; the nearest rail heads are Needamangalam and Thanjavur, with local buses and taxis to the village.
